messages.subject: Re: if else statement errors
messages.subject_clean: if else statement errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Steven,

Thanks for the question. The way you are trying to write model code is not supported. The reason is that model code is declarative (order doesn't matter) and is processed to establish the directed acyclic graph of relationships among model variables. if-then-else statements are not supported because they imply potentially changing or branching DAG relationships. Given that your IS.NA <http://IS.NA> vector is constant, there are several ways you could achieve what you want. One version would be with nested indexing. If I call your four cases A, B, C and D and you precompute their indices in advance and provide them in constants, you can do:

for(i in 1:n_caseA) {
  n[caseA_inds[i]] <- z[caseA_inds[i]]
  y[caseA_inds[i]] <- n[caseA_inds[i]]
}

for(i in 1:n_caseB) {
  n[caseB_inds[i]] <- z[caseB_inds[i]]
  y[caseB_inds[i]] ~ dbin(p,n[caseB_inds[i]])
}

etc.

Another version would be to define a nimbleFunction with some of the case splitting. However that would be trickier since sometimes you want y[i] to be stochastic and sometimes deterministic, so you'd still need multiple cases directly in the model code. Also the nested indexing approach above has the benefit that it tells the DAG specifically which relationships are where in the model.

A final relevant trick is to use logicals in arithmetic, like this:

n[i] <- z[i] + (IS.NA <http://IS.NA>[i-1]!=1)*(n[i-1]-y[i-1])

which looks like it covers your cases for n[i]. A disadvantage of this approach is that in the DAG, when algorithms are determining which nodes depend on which, it will always look like n[i] depends on n[i-1] and y[i-1] even when they don't really.

HTH
Perry

messages.subject: Building HMMs with continuous observation densities in NIMBLE
messages.subject_clean: Building HMMs with continuous observation densities in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
HI there,

I am looking to see if I can use NIMBLE to build a HMM that uses irregularly spaced observation times, that I would ideally like to model continuously as per Rushing (2023) (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2656.13902)

I was unable to identify how to do this in the documentation, is this possible? If so is there any documentation available on how to do this in NIMBLE?

Thanks,
Alex

messages.subject_clean: Building HMMs with continuous observation densities in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Dear Alex,
It should be possible. You may need to say more unless someone else can respond who is already familiar with the paper you've linked. One way people build HMMs is with dcat distributions and discrete latent states. Another way is with the marginal HMM distributions in nimbleEcology. If you need to get inside how the marginal HMM probabilities are calculated, you can look at the nimbleFunctions in the nimbleEcology source code, which read like R (and can be run and debugged uncompiled in R). I hope that points you in a starting direction.
Perry

Hi Pierre,

Sorry for the late reply but I have several problems over my desk right now.

I just wanted to let you know that the github development version that you suggested seems to fix the issue with HMC and our Leroux distribution, therefore I would appreciate so much if this was included in future versions of Nimble. At the end, I have tried to fit a simple model with Leroux distributed random effects with HMC and it works. Thus, as you suggested, the "%.s%" problem would be related to additional particular issues of my more complex version of the model (curiously this is a problem just for HMC but not for regular MCMC). In fact, my complex model has an array structure with inner (Leroux) multivariate nodes as the thread on the topic in November that you pointed out so it definitely seems a related issue. If I figure out something else about this issue I will let you know.

Finally, just a minor comment, since the installation of the provisional github version of nimble, Rstudio complains ("Error in fetch(key): lazy-load database '/home/.../nimble.rdb' is corrupt") every time that I try to access Nimble help either directly or indirectly (Rstudio tries to do it while writting code). This is not important since everything else seems to work fine, but at the end it results a bit annoying. I am just mentioning this just in case you should do something in this regard in future versions of Nimble that include the Leroux distribution fix just implemented.

Best wishes.

If it ever appears as in the error message you're seeing, it means something is wrong. Unfortunately, there is a bug where particular ways of using subsets of non-scalar stochastic nodes can cause this error. It is pretty unusual, but then again if it's arising from a model you need, it might not seem unusual at all. There was a thread on the topic in November <https://groups.google.com/u/3/g/nimble-users/c/ckgAe1KXvZE/m/wEVW9V2lBQAJ>. For now, the hope is that once you see the kind of situation that can create the problem, you might be able to change how you write your model to work around the problem. To diagnose further or make specific suggestions for you, I think we'd need to see your model code with at least the constants so that we can build the model (i.e. call nimbleModel) and inspect it. I could be wrong about the cause, but it does sound like the same issue as the November thread I linked.

messages.subject: Re: Incredibly Slow Model Runs
messages.subject_clean: Incredibly Slow Model Runs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Heather,

Thanks for posting this. I was not able to run your code because your zip file didn't include "bigmod.txt". I thought maybe "bigmod_test.txt" would be that so I changed the name but it didn't work and bigmod_test.txt looks like MCMC samples. (And I think files will be smaller saved via saveRDS, but no matter).

Let me make some general suggestions from reading your code.

help(buildMCMC) shows how you can use "time=TRUE" and then "getTimes()" from the compiled MCMC object to see the time spent in each sampler. This will give you an idea of where the computational costs are. Of course you also need to understand what is being computed when sampling a node, and this is usually given by model$getDependencies(node).

If you are confident the problem is your dmmm_psi_move_two, you can profile within that function using the function run.time. I see that help(run.time) doesn't give much, but it is in section 15.8 of the User Manual. You could just print the time of different sections of the code and see whether the huge for loops or the huge dmulti or both or something else is the slow part. There is a saying about pursuing code efficiency that it is better to profile than to guess what is slow, although you might have a good idea already.

Here are some ideas to try in changing how your model or nimbleFunctions are written.

You could remove psi from the model, pass eta_d to dmmm_psi_move_two, and manually use it there for the elements you need. psi looks like a large-sized expansion that duplicates the elements of eta_d only for purposes of using within dmmm_psi_move_two.

You could also remove the deterministic elements of n_post from the model and split the survivors[ss, t, q] into multiple declarations with some nested indexing to achieve what you have written. My guess would be that this is less of a win than removing psi from the model, but I can't be sure.

I'm not following all the details of dmmm_psi_move_two so I might miss the mark but here are some notes on that:

There is a cost to creating large objects such as all_prob and all_prob_norm. One thing you can do is create only one of them but re-use it, e.g.  all_prob[i,] <- all_prob[i,]/sum(all_prob[i,]), because after that you don't need the old all_prob. Another thing you can do is check out User Manual section 12.3 on user-defined distributions that include setup code and thus can retain their own internal variables (like a class). With this feature, you can write dmmm_psi_move_two and/or normalize_move so that they contain a *single* instance (each) of all_prob (created in setup code and assigned in run code using "<<-") that gets re-used each time without allocating+initializing and de-allocating. (The size of all_prob is (105*12)^2 * 8 / 2^20 = 12.1 MB, which is a lot to be doing many thousands or millions of times in MCMC.) Another thing you can do with this approach is hold gridDist in the user-defined function or distribution objects and thus keep it out of the model, where it only adds overhead.

You might be able to usefully combine normalize_move and dmmm_psi_move_two to form the large object(s) even less. You might be able to avoid repeating some of the work across t that does not depend on t. You might be able to compute the dmulti log probability manually as you get your hands on the relevant elements, to avoid forming large objects if their only purpose in existing as single objects is to pass the dmulti. In normalize_move, I think you could vectorize over k. Looking at the big nested loops in dmmm_psi_move_two, since there are (many?) impossible state transitions and so (guessing) many 0s in the large objects, I am wondering if there is a way to create smaller objects with a different indexing scheme.

HTH
Perry

On Wed, Mar 5, 2025 at 1:07 PM heather...@gmail.com <heather...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> I'm running a complex model that seems to be taking ages to run, even if I were to run it without data to perform a prior predictive check. Right now the model runs about 1 iteration per minute, which is agonizing.
>
> I suspect the problem is in the way I'm dealing with some latent multinomials in the model, but I can't figure out a way to speed it up so I'm reaching out for help.

>

I see that help(run.time) doesn't give much, but it is in section 15.8 of the User Manual. You could just print the time of different sections of the code and see whether the huge for loops or the huge dmulti or both or something else is the slow part. There is a saying about pursuing code efficiency that it is better to profile than to guess what is slow, although you might have a good idea already.

>
> You could remove psi from the model, pass eta_d to dmmm_psi_move_two, and manually use it there for the elements you need. psi looks like a large-sized expansion that duplicates the elements of eta_d only for purposes of using within dmmm_psi_move_two.

>
> I'm not following all the details of dmmm_psi_move_two so I might miss the mark but here are some notes on that:
>
> There is a cost to creating large objects such as all_prob and all_prob_norm. One thing you can do is create only one of them but re-use it, e.g.  all_prob[i,] <- all_prob[i,]/sum(all_prob[i,]), because after that you don't need the old all_prob. Another thing you can do is check out User Manual section 12.3 on user-defined distributions that include setup code and thus can retain their own internal variables (like a class). Another thing you can do with this approach is hold gridDist in the user-defined function or distribution objects and thus keep it out of the model, where it only adds overhead.
>

You might be able to avoid repeating some of the work across t that does not depend on t. You might be able to compute the dmulti log probability manually as you get your hands on the relevant elements, to avoid forming large objects if their only purpose in existing as single objects is to pass the dmulti. In normalize_move, I think you could vectorize over k. Looking at the big nested loops in dmmm_psi_move_two, since there are (many?) impossible state transitions and so (guessing) many 0s in the large objects, I am wondering if there is a way to create smaller objects with a different indexing scheme.

messages.subject_clean: eigen decomposition and type="double" when combined with dnorm vs dunif
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I've been trying to work an eigen decomposition into a nimble model, but am running into an issue. When I try to manipulate the extracted eigenvalue by adding or multiplying it by another parameter, I get the error "cannot coerce type 'closure' to vector of type 'double'."

But it only seems to happen when the other parameter is drawn from a normal distribution, and if I instead draw it from a uniform distribution, it works. I can't understand why those would produce different behavior. Simplified example below.
Thanks,
Franny

pumpCode <- nimbleCode({
  S ~ dunif(0,2)
  V ~ dunif(0,2)

  for (t in 1:T){
    D[1,1,t]<-0
    D[1,2,t]<-V
    D[1,3,t]<-V

    D[2,1,t]<-S
    D[2,2,t]<-0
    D[2,3,t]<-0

    D[3,1,t]<-0
    D[3,2,t]<-S
    D[3,3,t]<-S

    lambda_d[t]<-eigen(D[1:3,1:3,t])$values[1]

    C[t]~dpois(phi[t])
    log(phi[t])~dnorm(a+log(lambda_d[t]),sd=0.01)
  }

  #a~dunif(-1,1)
  a~dnorm(0,sd=0.0001)
})

S<-0.95
V<-0.25
T<-50
D<-matrix(c(0,V,V,S,0,0,0,S,S),byrow=T,nrow=3)
lambda_d<-eigen(D)$values[1]

C<-rep(0,T)
for (t in 2:T){
  log.lambda_d<-0.1+log(lambda_d)
  C[t]<-rpois(1,exp(log.lambda_d))
}

pumpInits <- list(S = 1, V = 1, a=0)
pumpConsts <- list(T=T)
pumpData <- list(C=C)

out<-nimbleMCMC(code = pumpCode, constants = pumpConsts,
                data = pumpData,inits=pumpInits,
                nchains = 1, niter = 60000,
                monitors = c("a"))

messages.body_plain:
Franny, this is a new one for sure.  The error is occurring at the stage of MCMC configuration, when the model object is inspected, and sampler choices are made for updating the dimensions of the model.  Apparently, the use of eigen(D)$values inside the model trips up the system for identifying conjugate dimensions of the model, thus giving the incomprehensible error that you're seeing.  The reason you don't see this when using a uniform prior, is the use of a uniform prior distribution precludes the possibility of possible conjugacy, so the conjugacy checking routine exits sooner.  However, the normal prior distribution allows the possibility of a conjugate relationship, so the conjugacy checking routine proceeds further - far enough to get itself into trouble.

This is something we'll have to look into, and fix.  In the meantime, you can use either prior distribution if you use the (slightly longer) workflow shown below.  I've updated the steps to be consistent with your original call to nimbleMCMC().  In the code below, you'll see the addition of "useConjugacy = FALSE", which skips all conjugacy checking entirely, so this problem doesn't arise.

Please let me know if this works for you.

Daniel

.......
.... earlier code here ....
.......

pumpInits <- list(S = 1, V = 1, a=0)
pumpConsts <- list(T=T)
pumpData <- list(C=C)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(pumpCode, pumpConsts, pumpData, pumpInits)

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, monitors = c("a"), useConjugacy = FALSE)

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

out <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, 60000)

messages.subject: Dynamic Indexing issues translating from JAGs to Nimble
messages.subject_clean: Dynamic Indexing issues translating from JAGs to Nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to translate a JAGs model to NIMBLE that models the number of vocalizations from acoustic recorders to estimate a species abundance. The reason for moving over to NIMBLE is that my abundance model is underdispersed and I don't have a way of handling it in JAGs, but could through a custom distribution in NIMBLE. However, I am running into some issue moving it over. The model uses a lot of dynamic indexing which I can deal with in part by using custom functions , but part of the model is a ztNB hurdle model and indexes through sites for surveys that have at least one vocalization.

Like so (JAGs code)

 # Site
  for (s in 1:S) {

    # Surveys with Vocalizations
    for (j in 1:J.r[s]) {

    # Zero Truncated Negative Binomial
    v[s, A.times[s, j]] ~ dpois((delta[s, A.times[s, j]] * N[s] + omega) * phi[s, A.times[s, j]] * y[s, A.times[s, j]]) T(1, )

    # PPC calls
    v.pred[s, j] ~ dpois((delta[s, A.times[s, j]] * N[s] + omega) * phi[s, A.times[s, j]] * y[s, A.times[s, j]]) T(1, )
    mu.v[s, j] <- ((delta[s, A.times[s, j]] * N[s] + omega) * phi[s, A.times[s, j]]) / (1 - exp(-1 * ((delta[s, A.times[s, j]] * N[s] + omega) * phi[s, A.times[s, j]])))
    resid.v[s, j] <- pow(pow(v[s, A.times[s, j]], 0.5) - pow(mu.v[s, j], 0.5), 2)
    resid.v.pred[s, j] <- pow(pow(v.pred[s, j], 0.5) - pow(mu.v[s, j], 0.5), 2)

    } # End J.r
  } # End S

The issue that I'm dealing with is figuring out a way to index through J.r,  where J.r contains the number of surveys at each acoustic site that contains at least 1 detected vocalization.
> J.r
 [1] 13 10  9 13 14  4 13 14  8 14 13 13 14 11 14  9 13  9 11 13 12  3  8
[24]  2  6  5  2

I know there are some other issues that I may be dealing with, but I'm not sure how to handle a work around for indexing through a vector in NIMBLE.

Suggestions and guidance appreciated.

Thanks!
-Dave

> Franny, this is a new one for sure.  The error is occurring at the stage of MCMC configuration, when the model object is inspected, and sampler choices are made for updating the dimensions of the model.  Apparently, the use of eigen(D)$values inside the model trips up the system for identifying conjugate dimensions of the model, thus giving the incomprehensible error that you're seeing.  The reason you don't see this when using a uniform prior, is the use of a uniform prior distribution precludes the possibility of possible conjugacy, so the conjugacy checking routine exits sooner. # Initial Values
inits <- list(
  # Abundance
  N = rep(1, S),
  beta0 = rnorm(1, 0, 1),
  beta1 = rnorm(1, 0, 1),
  beta2 = rnorm(1, 0, 1),

  # Detection
  alpha0 = 0,
  mu_alpha = 0.5,
  alpha1 = runif(1, 0, 1),
  alpha2 = rnorm(1, 0, 1),
  alpha3 = rnorm(1, 0, 1),

  # Vocalization
  omega = runif(1, 0, 1),
  gamma0 = log(10),

  # Survey random effect
  Jraneff = rep(0, J_A),
  mu_j = 1,
  tau_j = 1,

  # Overdispersion
  mu_phi = 1,
  tau_phi = 1,
  phi = matrix(1, nrow = S, ncol = J_A)

)

# -----------------------------
# Model Statement
# -----------------------------
acoustic_model <- nimbleCode({

  # ----------------------
  # Abundance Priors
  # ----------------------

  # Intercept
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 1)

  # Covariate effect
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  beta2 ~ dnorm(0, 1)

  # ------------------------
  # Detection Priors
  # ------------------------

  # Intercept
  alpha0 <- logit(mu_alpha)
  mu_alpha ~ dunif(0, 1)

  # True individuals
  alpha1 ~ dunif(0, 1000)

  # Covariate effect
  alpha2 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  alpha3 ~ dnorm(0, 1)

  # ------------------------
  # Call Rate Priors
  # ------------------------

  # False positive rate
  omega  ~ dunif(0, 1000)

  # Intercept
  gamma0 ~ dunif(log(1), log(60))

  # Survey random effect
  mu_j ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
  tau_j ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
  for (j in 1:n_days) {
    Jraneff[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau_j)
  }

  # Overdispersion
  mu_phi ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
  tau_phi ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)

  for (s in 1:S) {

    for (j in 1:J_A) {
      phi[s, j] ~ dgamma(mu_phi, tau_phi)
    }
  }

  # ------------------------
  # Likelihood and Process Model
  # ------------------------

  # Site
  for (s in 1:S) {

    # ---------------------------------
    # Abundance Submodel
    # ---------------------------------

    # Poisson
    log(lambda[s]) <- beta0 + beta1 * X_abund[s, 7] + beta2 * X_abund[s, 12]
    N[s] ~ dpois(lambda[s])

    # Survey
    for (j in 1:J_A) {

    # ---------------------------------
    # Detection Submodel
    # ---------------------------------

    # True Positives + Vegetation Density + Wind
    logit(p_a[s, j]) <- alpha0 + alpha1 * N[s] + alpha2 * X_abund[s, 21] + alpha3 * X_det[j, 2]

    # ---------------------------------
    # Call rate Submodel
    # ---------------------------------

    # Intercept + Survey Random Effect
    log(delta[s, j]) <- gamma0 + Jraneff[j]

    # ---------------------------------
    # Observations
    # ---------------------------------
    y[s, j] ~ dbin(p_a[s, j], 1)

    # ---------------------------------
    # True Positives
    # ---------------------------------
    tp[s, j] <- delta[s, j] * N[s] / (delta[s, j] * N[s] + omega)

    } # End J

    # ---------------------------------
    # Vocalizations
    # ---------------------------------

    # Surveys with Vocalizations
    for (j in 1:J_r[s]) {

      # Zero Truncated Negative Binomial

      v[s, A_times[s, j]] ~ T(dpois((delta[s, A_times[s, j]] * N[s] + omega) * phi[s, A_times[s, j]] * y[s, A_times[s, j]]), 1, )

      }# End J_R

  } # End S

  # ------------------------
  # Manual Validation
  # ------------------------

  for (s in 1:S_val) {

    for (j in 1:J_val[s]) {

      K[s, j] ~ dbin(tp[sites_a[s], j], v[sites_a[s], val_times[s, j]])
      k[s, val_times[s, j]] ~ dhyper_nimble(K[s, j], v[sites_a[s], val_times[s, j]] - K[s, j], n[s, val_times[s, j]])
    } # End J
  } # End S

  # -------------------------------------------
  # Derive Parameters
  # -------------------------------------------

  # Abundance
  N_tot <- sum(N[1:S])
})
# ---------------------------- End Model ----------------------------

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave,

Glad we can help get you started. First, as the message states, it is not necessarily an error to not initialize your model fully.

The nodes listed as not initialized are some lifted nodes (see our User Manual at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org> if you need background on lifted nodes -- basically nodes nimble has inserted to implement your model) and K.

It looks like K is a posterior predictive node (from your code comments), so it shouldn't be a problem that it's not initialized.

The first lifted node name is a text conversion of "(delta[s, A_times[s, j]] * N[s] + omega) * phi[s, A_times[s, j]] * y[s, A_times[s, j]])". The second is a text conversion of "v[sites_a[s], val_times[s, j]] - K[s, j], n[s, val_times[s, j]]". The second one depends on K[s, j], so it makes sense that if K[s, j] is not initialized neither is something that depends on it.

I'm not following in enough detail to see what is up with the first one, but you can start inspecting the model as a way to find out.
E.g.
model$calculate("v") #calculate all of it
model$calculate("v[1, ]") #calcualte part of it, etc., to isolate where it is using values that are not initialized
model$getParam("v[1, 1]", "mean") # inspect directly its mean parameter value
model$N # and/or look at variables that are used in the calculation
model$phi #etc.

HTH
Perry

messages.subject: Compiled and non-compiled functions return different values
messages.subject_clean: Compiled and non-compiled functions return different values
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

One thing I have noticed recently that has made me a bit nervous is that compiled and non-compiled code can return different values. For instance,

library(nimble)

testf <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(y = double(1)) { # type declarations
    for(i in 1:4){
      y <- y+2
    }
    return(i)
    returnType(double(0)) # return type declaration
  } )

testf(1)

ctestf <- compileNimble(testf)

ctestf(1)

Here, testf(1) returns 4 and ctestf(1) returns 5. It appears when compiling that the for loop index gets increased by 1 after the loop.

This has made me nervous because I write my own samplers. I always test these samplers in R so I can go line by line. I am not sure how to test the compiled samplers to make sure they return the same sampled, and other, values. Anyone know how to do this?

Also, does anyone know other important examples where there would be differences in the compiled and non-compiled code?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Compiled and non-compiled functions return different values
messages.subject_clean: Compiled and non-compiled functions return different values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk,
That's an interesting catch. The exit behavior of the for-loop index differs (but result y shouldn't differ). Often for-loop indices are later ignored, but sometimes one relies on their exit value, so this could matter. There are some other differences in compiled vs uncompiled behavior, notably that in compiled code non-scalar numeric arguments will be passed by reference. There shouldn't be glaring differences in math.
One way to test your own samplers would be to call them manually (outside of the MCMC), after setting the seed for reproducibility. Off the top of my head I can suggest two ways to do this. The first would be to build the sampler on its own (not within an MCMC). For that purpose it might be easier to remove uses of the mvSamples, since those are set up from the MCMC (i.e. buildMCMC). Then you could compile the sampler object directly and, if you set a seed, set values in the model, and call the sampler, all with the uncompiled objects (model + sampler) and then (after re-setting to the same seed) with the compiled objects (model + sampler),  you should get identical behavior. The second would be to do
nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions = TRUE)
(always worth a chuckle at that long but accurate name ;-) )
Then you can use the samplers as they were built in the MCMC (including mvSamples etc). You should be able to access samplers (compiled or uncompiled) by
MCMC$samplerFunctions[[i]]
where MCMC was returned from buildMCMC and i is a choice of which sampler you want to look at. E.g. you can set the state of the model, then the seed, and then manually call one iteration of sampler i:
MCMC$samplerFunctions[[i]]$run()
or inspect its internals
MCMC$samplerFunctions[[i]]$scale
In the uncompiled MCMC, you can check the target node of a sampler to be sure it's the sampler of interest
MCMC$samplerFunctions[[i]]$target
A final approach to checking on what your own sampler is doing is to define a nimbleRcall to some R function and call it from the run code of your sampler. Then put a browser() in the R function (or debug() it). Then when your compiled code is running, it will call your R function and you'll get into a browser, from which you can inspect the state of the compiled model etc (e.g. to see what proposal value was used, or what calculations were done). You can also access sampler setup (member) variables as described above. If you need to look at local variables, you'd have to pass them as arguments to the nimbleRcall.
HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
I've got a model that runs just fine with MCMC but I'd like to try HMC, and I'm getting a compilation error associated with the step() function when I set buildDerivs = TRUE.

The offending line of code in the nimble model is:
date_idx[i, k+1] <- sum(step(det_time[i, k + 1] - date_vec[]))

In short, sum(step(...)) finds the appropriate index (date_idx) in a vector of dates (date_vec[] = days since 1970-01-01) associated with a continuous datetime (det_time).

Here's the compilation error:
P_3_ttCjsCode_MID_4_nfCode.cpp: In member function 'virtual CppAD::AD<double> date_idx_L19_UID_96::calculate_ADproxyModel(const indexedNodeInfo&) const':
  P_3_ttCjsCode_MID_4_nfCode.cpp:3087:387:

error: invalid 'static_cast' from type 'CppAD::AD<double> (*)(CppAD::AD<double>)' to type 'CppAD::AD<int> (*)(CppAD::AD<double>)'
3087 | stoch_ind_set((**ADproxyModel_date_idx), (ARG1_INDEXEDNODEINFO__.info[0]) - 1, (ARG1_INDEXEDNODEINFO__.info[2]) - 1) =
      ((stoch_ind_get((**ADproxyModel_det_time), (ARG1_INDEXEDNODEINFO__.info[0]) - 1, (ARG1_INDEXEDNODEINFO__.info[2]) - 1) -
      ((eigenBlock_oPADproxyModel_date_vec_comma_1to366_cP).block(0, 0, 366, 1)).array())
      .unaryExpr(std::function< CppAD::AD<int>(CppAD::AD<double>) >( static_cast<CppAD::AD<int> (*)(CppAD::AD<double>)>(&nimDerivs_nimStep)))).sum();

There seems to be an issue with type conversion from between integer and double.  I can see that nimStep produces an integer-valued vector (the R version), so I wonder if that's part of the issue.

Any suggestions for how to solve this problem would be much appreciated!  Also, I can provide a reproduceable example if the issue isn't immediately apparent or is rooted deeper in the model.

Thanks!

This is for a time-varying covariate CJS model model where the detection time (det_time) is sometimes latent for unobserved individuals.  So det_time is sampled given the distribution of observed times of detected individuals in order to integrate over unobserved time-varying covariates. It's a bit more complicated, but that's the gist.

messages.subject_clean: Compile errors when using nested nimble functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I'm trying to construct a custom HMM distribution using the dHMM function in the nimbleEcology package. See below for example.
len <- 5 # length of dataset
dat <- c(1,2,1,1,2) # A vector of observations
init <- c(1, 0, 0) # A vector of initial state probabilities
probObs <- t(array( # A matrix of observation probabilities
  c(1, 0,
    0, 1,
    0.2, 0.8), c(2, 3)))
probTrans <- t(array( # A matrix of transition probabilities
  c(0.6, 0.3, 0.1,
    0, 0.7, 0.3,
    0, 0, 1), c(3,3)))

dHMM(x=dat, probOb=probObs, probTrans=probTrans, init=init, len=5, log=TRUE)

I want to create a distribution that conditions on the fact that the markov chain cannot stay in state 1 and must at some point move to 2. So I define the nimble function

dHMMna1 <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1), init = double(1), probObs = double(2),
               probTrans = double(3), len = integer(),
               checkRowSums = integer(0, default = 1),
               log = integer(0, default = 0)){
  du <- dHMM(x=x, probOb=probObs, probTrans=probTrans, init=init, len=len, log=1)
  ones <- rep(1,len)
  dc <- dHMM(x=ones, probOb=probObs, probTrans=probTrans, init=init, len=len, log=0)
  logL <- du - log(1-dc)
  returnType(double())
  if (log) return(logL)
  return(exp(logL))
})

which works beautifully and works within nimbleModel(), etc provided I register it. However when I compile it with compileNimble(), either the function or the model. I get the C++ error:
P_9_nc_MID_5_nfCode.cpp:318:6: error: no matching function for call to 'rcFun_nimbleEcology52'
du = rcFun_nimbleEcology52(ARG1_x_, ARG2_init_, ARG3_probObs_, ARG4_probTrans_, ARG5_len_, 1, 1);
     ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
P_9_nc_MID_5_nfCode.cpp:60:9: note: candidate function not viable: no known conversion from 'NimArr<3, double>' to 'NimArr<2, double

I'm pretty new to nimble, so, maybe I'm just making a rookie mistake. I came across this other thread,
https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/Y4LxSU9Iyw0/m/gsQ4G33XBAAJ
but there doesn't seem to be a solution there.

-Devin

messages.subject: Tricking nimble into doing polya-gamma for multicategorical logit
messages.subject_clean: Tricking nimble into doing polya-gamma for multicategorical logit
messages.body_plain:
The polya-gamma sampler works great for logistic regression. However, it's limited in that it can only handle bernoulli or binomial likelihoods.

I'm trying to trick it using the stick-breaking representation of the categorical distribution (so it boils down to a product of Bernoullis).

Ultimately, I need this to work where the categories are latent (e.g., a mixture model), so I figured I would try to see if I can get it to work in an i.i.d. setting first. The model compiles just fine, and Nimble recognizes conjugacy everywhere. However, the results don't reflect the truth at all.

I'm not sure if it's a tiny bug, a flaw in the logic, or if this is just a current limitation (that can hopefully be fixed in the future). If it can be figured out, however, it opens the possibility for Nimble to be used with e.g., logit stick breaking processes.

Below is my code:

library(nimble)
code <- nimbleCode({
  ## Stick-breaking probabilities
  for ( k in 1:(K-1) )
    v[k] ~ dbeta(0.5, 0.5)

  w[1:K] <- stick_breaking(v[1:(K-1)])

  ## Priors for mu
  for ( k in 1:K )
    mu[k] ~ dnorm(0, 1)

  for ( i in 1:n ) {
    size[i, 1] <- 1            ## There is always stick for first component
    z[i, 1] ~ dbern(v[1])      ## First stick always random
    for ( k in 2:(K-1) ) {
      size[i, k]  <- size[i, k-1] - z[i, k-1]       ## = 1 if no success drawn yet and 0 if there has
      ztilde[i, k] ~ dbern(v[k])                    ## Latent Bernoulli
      z[i, k]      <- size[i, k] * ztilde[i,k]      ## z[i, k] = 0 if there is no stick left
    }
    y[i] ~ dnorm( inprod(z[i, 1:K], mu[1:K]) , 1)
  }
})

n  = 300
mu = c(-10, 0, 10)
p  = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.25)
z  = rcat(n, p)
y  = rnorm(n, mu[z], 1)

constants = list(n = n, K = length(p))
data = list(y = rnorm(n))
inits = list(v = runif(K-1), mu = rnorm(K), z = cbind(1, matrix(0, n, K-1)) )
inits$ztilde = inits$z
model = nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)
cmodel = compileNimble(model)
mcmcConf = configureMCMC(model, monitors = c('mu', 'w'))
mcmc = buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
cmcmc = compileNimble(mcmc, project = cmodel)

fit = runMCMC(cmcmc, 12000, 2000)

messages.subject: can deterministic nodes be data?
messages.subject_clean: can deterministic nodes be data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, apologies if this is a silly question but I'm very new to NIMBLE. I'm looking at a model where the observations are a deterministic function of model parameters and something stochastic: observation x[i]=f(theta,y[i]) where theta is a model parameter, and y[i] is stochastic (normally distributed in fact). If, instead, I had x[i]=f(y[i]) then I could calculate f^{-1}(x[i]) and focus on modelling these as normally distributed, but it is not so straightforward because of the dependence on the model parameter theta. So, is it possible to have deterministic nodes as data? the manual says not. Or is it possible to work around this issue somehow?
Thanks,
Stephen

messages.subject: Re: can deterministic nodes be data?
messages.subject_clean: can deterministic nodes be data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stephen,

No, it is not possible to have a deterministic node be data.

In most cases I have seen where people want to do this (but there are exceptions), a rearrangement of thinking results in seeing the actual observed datum as stochastic. For example, if y[i] follows a distribution, then the function f(theta, y[i]) follows a distribution that can be derived from y[i]'s distribution. If you can write that out, then you can code it in a nimbleFunction and use that as a user-defined distribution for x[i]. Of course, that assumes y[i] is unobserved.

If you really need to work around the system more, another trick is to provide a dummy data value that you declare to be a stochastic node with a user-defined distribution, and then calculate whatever log probability you want to contribute to the model.
Example:
dtricky <- nimbleFunction(...) # see user manual on writing a user-defined distribution
Model code:
dummy[i] ~ dtricky(x[i], theta, y[i])
This results in calls to dtricky as:
<contribution to log probability or likelihood> = dtricky(dummy[i], x[i], theta, y[i])

So dummy[i] can serve simply to place a log probability calculation in the DAG that will be seen as depending on x[i], theta, and y[i].

HTH
Perry

messages.subject: announcing the nimbleMacros package and the use of macros in nimble models
messages.subject_clean: announcing the nimbleMacros package and the use of macros in nimble models
messages.body_plain:
Dear NIMBLE users,

Recent versions of NIMBLE now include the ability to use macros in models. A NIMBLE macro is a succinct syntax that expands to create the NIMBLE model code for part or all of a model.

We recently released the first version of the `nimbleMacros` package, which provides an initial set of macros available to users and developers. As an example, one could set up the code for a linear mixed effects model by using the `LM` ("linear model") macro like this:

```
library(nimbleMacros)

code <- nimbleCode({
  LM(weight[1:N] ~ Time + (1|Chick))
})

```

with the formula syntax mimicking that of the lme4 package. After building the model based on the `code` object, you can see the model code produced after the macro is expanded with `model$getCode()`. The nimbleMacros package also includes macros for creating linear predictors and for loops, and we plan to add additional macros in the future.

Developers can use the tools in `nimble` itself to create their own macros. See Section 12.4 of the NIMBLE user manual <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-user-defined.html#sec:user-macros>, the `nimbleMacros` vignette <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nimbleMacros/vignettes/nimbleMacros.html>, or  `help(buildMacro)` for more information.

-Chris (for the NIMBLE development team)

If I rework the code to function with a "regular" loop, e.g., fot(i in 1:K){..} everything works on both sides. I'm not sure if this is a known issue. On Thursday, March 13, 2025 at 3:37:21 PM UTC-6 Perry de Valpine wrote:
> Hi Dirk,
> That's an interesting catch. The exit behavior of the for-loop index differs (but result y shouldn't differ). Often for-loop indices are later ignored, but sometimes one relies on their exit value, so this could matter. There are some other differences in compiled vs uncompiled behavior, notably that in compiled code non-scalar numeric arguments will be passed by reference. There shouldn't be glaring differences in math.
> One way to test your own samplers would be to call them manually (outside of the MCMC), after setting the seed for reproducibility. Off the top of my head I can suggest two ways to do this. The first would be to build the sampler on its own (not within an MCMC). For that purpose it might be easier to remove uses of the mvSamples, since those are set up from the MCMC (i.e. buildMCMC). Then you could compile the sampler object directly and, if you set a seed, set values in the model, and call the sampler, all with the uncompiled objects (model + sampler) and then (after re-setting to the same seed) with the compiled objects (model + sampler),  you should get identical behavior. The second would be to do
> nimbleOptions(buildInterfacesForCompiledNestedNimbleFunctions = TRUE)
> (always worth a chuckle at that long but accurate name ;-) )
> Then you can use the samplers as they were built in the MCMC (including mvSamples etc). You should be able to access samplers (compiled or uncompiled) by
> MCMC$samplerFunctions[[i]]
> where MCMC was returned from buildMCMC and i is a choice of which sampler you want to look at. E.g. you can set the state of the model, then the seed, and then manually call one iteration of sampler i:
> MCMC$samplerFunctions[[i]]$run()
> or inspect its internals
> MCMC$samplerFunctions[[i]]$scale
> In the uncompiled MCMC, you can check the target node of a sampler to be sure it's the sampler of interest
> MCMC$samplerFunctions[[i]]$target
> A final approach to checking on what your own sampler is doing is to define a nimbleRcall to some R function and call it from the run code of your sampler. Then put a browser() in the R function (or debug() it). Then when your compiled code is running, it will call your R function and you'll get into a browser, from which you can inspect the state of the compiled model etc (e.g. to see what proposal value was used, or what calculations were done). You can also access sampler setup (member) variables as described above. If you need to look at local variables, you'd have to pass them as arguments to the nimbleRcall.

messages.subject: Help debugging convergence problems with MCEM
messages.subject_clean: Help debugging convergence problems with MCEM
messages.body_plain:
I've set up a model to use with MCEM.  I can get the bootstrap filter working with this model and it compiles, however, when running the EM algorithm it diverges:

```

## Compilation
brownianModel <-
  nimbleModel(brownianModelCode1,
              constants=list(N=N,J=J,NT=NT,
                             deltaT=deltaT,
                             tasks=tasks),
              dimensions=list(p=c(N,NT,3L)),
              inits=bminits,check=FALSE,
              data=list(y=y),
              buildDerivs = TRUE)

cBrownianModel <- compileNimble(brownianModel,showCompilerOutput=FALSE)
brownianMCEM <- buildMCEM(model=brownianModel,latentNodes="theta")
cBrownianMCEM <- compileNimble(brownianMCEM,project=brownianModel)

## Run MCEM (this step fails)
cBrownianMCEM$findMLE(initM=1000)
```

This last gives an error:

```

## Error in cBrownianMCEM$findMLE(initM = 1000) :
##  Non-finite log-likelihood occurred; the MCEM optimization cannot continue.
## Please check the state of the compiled model (accessible as 'name_of_model$CobjectInterface')
## and determine which parameter values are causing the invalid log-likelihood by calling
## 'calculate' with subsets of the model parameters
## (e.g., 'name_of_model$CobjectInterface$calculate('y[3]')'
## to see if node 'y[3]' is the cause of the problem). Note that if your model is maximizing
## over parameters whose bounds are not constant (i.e., depend on other parameters),
## this is one possible cause of such problems; in that case you might try running the MCEM
## without bounds, by setting 'forceNoConstraints = TRUE'.

```

This error message doesn't reflect the current version of nimble, as `cBrownianMCEM` does not have a
`$CobjectInterface` field, although `brownianMCEM$.CobjectInterface` is an object. But this
doesn't have a `$calculate()` method.

The `brownianModel` and `cBrownianModel` objects do have a `calculate()` method, but I'm
not sure that their parameter values are referencing.

Q1. How do I access the values at the point in which MCEM blew up to diagnose the problem?

Q2. Is there a way to turn on tracing for the MCEM algorithm?

There seems to be an undocumented `optimControl` parameter which can be set in `control`,
but tracing at that level would trace within the M-step and I want to trace the EM algorithm.
(As that error message clearly needs to be fixed, I posted Issue #1535 on github. I've got the complete
model and some test data there if you are curious).

Thanks,
--Russell

--
Russell Almond
https://ralmond.net/

Hi Ethan,

I ran your code, and you have identified a bug. I've made it an issue on the github:
Polya-Gamma Sampler unchecked zero-inflation · Issue #1536 · nimble-dev/nimble <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/issues/1536>

In the sampler set up we do the zero inflation calculations only when check=TRUE. However, if check = FALSE and there is zero inflation then an error is thrown. We will try and get it fixed soon, and I will post an update here. Thanks for sharing the example.

Paul

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ethan,
A follow up on your error. I have started drafting the sampler to recognize the stick_breaking transformation for when using dmulti or dcat. But in the meantime, I got your example working.

This line here

logit(v[1:n, 1:(K-1)]) <- X[1:n, 1:p] %*% beta[1:p, 1:(K-1)]

results in our sampler including all logit probabilities in the probability nodes and it becomes falsely identified as zero inflated.

Defining the logit probabilities in a loop removes that issue and the example you sent runs without a problem.
  for( i in 1:(K-1) )
    logit(v[1:n, i]) <- X[1:n, 1:p] %*% beta[1:p, i]

Another small note is to put check = FALSE in the control list:
mcmcConf$addSampler(varname, 'polyagamma', control = list(fixedDesignColumns=TRUE,  check = FALSE))

Let me know if this works for you or if you have any other questions.
Paul

messages.subject: Re: Help debugging convergence problems with MCEM
messages.subject_clean: Help debugging convergence problems with MCEM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Russell,

Thanks for the question.

Some clarifications: buildMCEM will by default build an MCMC with default samplers for the MCMC steps of the MCEM iterations. You can provide your own MCMC configuration function if you want to change that. But it would not by default build a particle filter, so I wasn't clear what you were referring to (or simply if you were referring to an entirely separate case but using the same model).

The <name_of_model> in the error message would be referring to the model object, i.e. brownianModel, not the algorithm objects BrownianMCEM (uncompiled) or cBrownianMCEM (compiled). After calling compileNimble, then brownianModel$CobjectInterface should exist. But that will simply be cBrownianModel, which in your workflow you already have your hands on, so you do not need to use brownianModel$CobjectInterface to find it. Since the compiled algorithm will use the compiled model, the suggestion is that you can inspect the compiled model (cBrownianModel) to look for where there is a non-finite log probability (called log-likelihood in the message). E.g. you can look at node values (cBrownianModel$x or whatever) or calculations (cBrownianModel$calculate("x") ).

I don't see a built-in way to trace the MCEM iteration by iteration, but here are a few ideas:
(i) Make a small version of the problem and run MCEM uncompiled. Then you can set debug(brownianMCEM$findMLE) and step through it.
(ii) Make a copy of the source code and modify it. Copy buildMCEM from the source code. <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCEM_build.R> Rename it in your own local code file (also change the "name=" argument). When you run it the setup code may break because it may use non-exported functions. Insert nimble::: in front of those to access them from the nimble namespace. You might also need to copy, rename, and insert nimble::: as needed in other nimbleFunctions used by buildMCEM. Define a nimbleRcall and put browser() inside the called R function (or debug() it). Insert calls to that nimbleRcall inside the findMLE method's source code. Then you will be thrown from the compiled algorithm into a browser() where you've inserted those calls, and you can inspect the compiledModel to see what is going on with it. You could also insert print statements etc.
(iii) Look up the documentation in the User Manual or help(nimOptim) about providing your own method to optim. (In help(nimOptim), this is described as "experimental" but should work fine). You can provide an R function that simply makes your own call to a regular optimizer (e.g. optim) but also lets you generate output, insert browser() statements, or do other debugging).

HTH
Perry

Hi Perry,
thanks for the reply. Below you can see the model that I want to implement.

The code that I have so far is this:

code <- nimbleCode({
  # Priors for each asset
  for (i in 1:N) {
    phi[i] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd=0.3), -0.99, 0.99) # Persistence factor
    sigma_h[i] ~ dinvgamma(1, scale=0.5)  # Std of transitory volatility
  }
  sv[1] <- 1 # Normalize first factor to 1
  for (i in 2:N) {
    sv[i] ~ dnorm(1, sd=0.5) # Scale factor for permanent component
  }
  sm[1] <- 1 # Normalize first factor to 1
  for (i in 2:N) {
    sm[i] ~ dnorm(1, sd=0.5)  # Scale factor for jumps in mean
  }

  # Priors for constant variables
  sigma_eta ~ dinvgamma(2, scale=2)  # Std of permanent component
  sigma_nu ~ dinvgamma(2, scale=2)  # Std of jumps in mean
  p_v ~ dbeta(2,5)  # Probability of volatility jumps
  p_m ~ dbeta(2,3)  # Probability of jumps in mean

  # Priors for each time step
  mu[1] ~ dnorm(-10, sd=0.2)  # Initial state of permanent volatility
  for (t in 2:T) {
    mu[t] ~ dnorm(mu[t-1], sd=delta_v[t]*sigma_eta)
  }
  for (t in 1:T) {
     u_v[t] ~ dunif(0, 1)
     u_m[t] ~ dunif(0, 1)
     z_m[t] ~ dnorm(0, 1)  # Standard normal innovations for jumps in mean
     delta_v[t] <- step(u_v[t]-(1-p_v))
     delta_m[t] <- step(u_m[t]-(1-p_m))
  }

  # Priors for each asset and time step
  for (i in 1:N) {
    h[1, i] ~ dnorm(0, sd=sigma_h[i]/sqrt(1-phi[i]*phi[i]))  # Initial state of transitory volatility
    for (t in 2:T) {
      h[t, i] ~ dnorm(phi[i] * h[t-1,i], sd=sigma_h[i])  # Transitory component
    }
  }
  for (i in 1:N) {
    for (t in 1:T) {
      gamma[t, i] <- sm[i] * delta_m[t] * sigma_nu * z_m[t]  # Jump process in mean
    }
  }

  # Loop over assets
  for (i in 1:N) {
    for (t in 1:T) {
      y[t, i] ~ dnorm(gamma[t, i]*exp((h[t, i] + sv[i] * mu[t]) / 2), sd = exp((h[t, i] + sv[i] * mu[t]) / 2))  # Observation equation
    }
  }
})

The parts I am not sure about are highlighted in red. Defining mu the way I did it here does not work properly, as it prevents sigma_eta from updating over iterations. So I was wondering how to properly incorporate the Bernoulli variable delta_v into the mu equation.

Further, according to the model the Bernoulli processes are sampled using auxiliary uniform variables and take on value one if the uniform variables exceed a threshold that is aligned with the parameters p_m and p_v. Therefore, I decided to use 1-p_v and 1-p_m as thresholds but I am open for other suggestions.

Lastly the observation equation contains the conditional volatility in the mean so far, which I am not sure about. Should I only use gamma as conditional mean?

Thank you very much for any suggestions!
Best regards
JM

messages.subject: Re: Model Jumps in Stochastic Volatility Model
messages.subject_clean: Model Jumps in Stochastic Volatility Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi JM,

I can't follow all the details (I'm not sure your code directly reflects the equations you provided, but I see it comes close) but I can try to reply.

If you want the deltas to follow a Bernoulli, you can do it directly as:
delta_v[t] ~ dbern(p_v)
Alternatively:
delta_v[t] ~ dbinom(size = 1, prob = p_v)

The declarations like

 sv[i] ~ dnorm(1, sd=0.5)

were curious to me because they are not in your equations and it seems unusual to give a prior mean of 1, but anyway that's not what you're asking about.

I guess the problem with

mu[t] ~ dnorm(mu[t-1], sd=delta_v[t]*sigma_eta)

might occur because if delta_v[t] is 0, the log probability must be either Inf (if mu[t] == mu[t-1]) or -Inf (otherwise).
MCMC updates of the mu[t] values will never make them perfectly equal, so you'll never be able to have delta_v[t] == 0 accepted in MCMC. (Also I don't see eta_t represented in your code.)
You might be able to set this up by adding the second term of equation (3) to mu[t-1] and using the reversible jump (see configureRJ) with delta_v[t] as the indicator variable. I'm not completely sure. That does create a potentially inefficient way to write a state-space model in nimble code because then the sequence of states would be deterministic sums of stochastic nodes, such that updating at time t requires would calculation of all subsequent times. Another more involved option would be to write a joint MCMC sampler for delta_v[t] and mu[t], if you are comfortable creating MCMC samplers. The User Manual covers the software side of this in section 15.5.

The questions about how to use an auxiliary variable (if you don't want to use dbern or dbinom directly) or the correct observation model seem to be more about the statistics and not the software, and I don't know these models well enough to respond. Someone else might chime in, but generally our support on this list is on the software mechanics. Let me know if I'm not seeing the questions clearly.

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Dear Frédéric,

A variable in a model does not necessarily have a prior. But I think we should be talking about nodes, because a variable is just a label for an object that may contain one or more nodes. A node that is stochastic and is not data will have a prior.

Scalar constants are absorbed completely without creating a variable. Non-scalar constants become variables.

In your example, `matrix_exp_quiz_PM[i, 2:6]` (for each i) will be labeled as a right-hand-side only (or RHSonly) node, meaning it does not have a declaration in which it appears on the left-hand-side of `<-` or `~`. A typical example is a covariate or explanatory variable.

If you use `model$getNodeNames`, you will find an option to include RHS only nodes or not (default not).

With clarification on these points, are you able to modify your use of the model to get the correct calculations done as you need?

Perry

messages.subject: Re: Building HMMs with continuous observation densities in NIMBLE
messages.subject_clean: Building HMMs with continuous observation densities in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
The trick is to use an index for observation times (which could be different for each individual if you are working with panel data like I am), and pass in a constant array of time difference to work with.  Here is the heart of a simple model for non-stationary Brownian motion.

```
brownianModelCode1 <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1L:N) {
    theta[i,1L] ~ dnorm(mu_0,sigma_0)
    for (it in 2L:(NT)) {
      theta[i,it] ~dnorm(theta[i,it-1L] + growthRate[i]*deltaT[i,it-1L],
                                      growthSD[i]*sqrt(deltaT[i,it-1L]))
    }
  }
## Emission model part omitted.
```

I'm not familiar with Rushing(2003), but I hope this gets you pointed in the right direction.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Russell,

I think the most proximate issue is that IrtItemPool should have enableDerivs  turned on for run. I think also that task should be declared as double, not integer, because all model variables are doubles. It doesn’t usually matter, but for AD (yes, that is the issue) it does. And I think you’ll need to check out ADbreak to stop derivative tracking of task inside run. There is a subsection of the AD chapter of the user manual that tries to cover this. I am away from my computer so can’t check on other things that might come up using AD with nimbleFunctionVirtual. I think since task is constant, another option would to use if-then cases within IrtItemPool$run to call other nimbleFunctions, also with enableDerivs set.

HTH,
Perry

On Sat, Mar 29, 2025 at 4:12 PM Russell Almond <russell....@gmail.com> wrote:

> I'm having trouble compiling a model which I think has something with how I'm declaring something.  The idea is that observations by various persons and time points are coming from different distributions, so I've set up an array `tasks[i,it]` (passed as a constant) saying which one to use at each time point.  I've also set up a function list to do the indirection:
>
> ```
> Irt <- nimbleFunctionVirtual(
>   run = function(theta=double(0)) {returnType(double(1,3))}
> )
> IrtItemPool <- nimbleFunction(
>   setup = function (irtmod,plist) {
>     J <- length(plist)
>     itemfuns <- nimbleFunctionList(Irt)
>     for (task in 1:J)
>         itemfuns[[task]] <- do.call(irtmod,plist[task])
>     setupOutputs(J,itemfuns)
>   },
>   run = function(task=integer(0),theta=double(0)) {
>     returnType(double(1,3))
>     return(itemfuns[[task]]$run(theta))
>   })
> ```
>
> So the idea is that `theta` is the critical parameter, and the `ItemPool` function selects the `ItemFunction` according to the discrete task argument.
>
> Here is the model code:
>
> ```
> constGrowthCode <- nimbleCode({
>   for (i in 1L:N) {
>     theta[i,1L] ~ dnorm(mu0,sig0)
>     for (it in 2L:(NT)) {
>       theta[i,it] ~dnorm(theta[i,it-1L] + growthRate, growthSD)
>     }
>   }
>
>   for (i in 1L:N) {
>     for (it in 1L:NT) {
>       p[i,it,1L:3L] <- itempool$run(tasks[i,it],theta[i,it])
>       y[i,it] ~dcat(p[i,it,])
>     }
>   }
> # Priors omitted
> )
> ```
> However, this gives me an error:
> ```
> P_16_constGrowt_MID_27_nfCode.cpp:1092:42: error: cannot convert ‘TYPE_’ {aka ‘CppAD::AD<double>’} to ‘double’ 1092 | Interm_690 = (*itempool).run(Interm_688, Interm_689); | ^~~~~~~~~~ | | | TYPE_ {aka CppAD::AD<double>}
> ```
>
> I don't understand how the compiler is deciding whether to map a variable to a double or an AD<double>. Does this have something to do with the automatic differentiation?
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Perry,

I thank you for your answer. The trouble I have is that matrix_exp_quiz_PM is in the constants of the Nimble model (i.e. in the list of constants other than data provided to Nimble). Can it then be considered as a variable? I understood that no. But maybe I did not catch something.

Sincerely,

Frédéric

Le mercredi 26 mars 2025 à 20:07:04 UTC+1, Perry de Valpine a écrit :
> Dear Frédéric,
>
> A variable in a model does not necessarily have a prior. But I think we should be talking about nodes, because a variable is just a label for an object that may contain one or more nodes. A node that is stochastic and is not data will have a prior.
>
> Scalar constants are absorbed completely without creating a variable. Non-scalar constants become variables.
>
> In your example, `matrix_exp_quiz_PM[i, 2:6]` (for each i) will be labeled as a right-hand-side only (or RHSonly) node, meaning it does not have a declaration in which it appears on the left-hand-side of `<-` or `~`. A typical example is a covariate or explanatory variable.
>
> If you use `model$getNodeNames`, you will find an option to include RHS only nodes or not (default not).
>
> With clarification on these points, are you able to modify your use of the model to get the correct calculations done as you need?
>
> Perry
>
>
> On Wed, Mar 26, 2025 at 3:23 AM frederic....@gmail.com <frederic....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello,
> >
> > I have come to a problem of calculations on a MCMC nimble model based on nimbleFunctions that seems to be explained by the following problem: when adding in my model nimble Code the following element:
> > +sum(eta[1:5] * matrix_exp_quiz_PM[i,2:6])
> > - together with priors for the new parameter eta- Nimble identifies matrix_exp_quiz_PM as a variable - through e.g. the command: CModel[[i]]$getVarNames() where CModel  is the result of the function nimble::compileNimble - although it is provided in the Model Constants list - and does not have a prior.
> >
> > The MCMC works fine but subsequent calculations not apparently due to this problem.
> >
> > Sincerely,
> >
> > Frédéric

messages.subject: Re: Nimble creating a variable from a constant
messages.subject_clean: Nimble creating a variable from a constant
messages.body_plain:
Hi Frédéric,

Perry is out for the week, so let me see if I can help.  Even if you are providing `matrix_exp_quiz_PM` in`constants`, nimble treats it as a variable because it is not a scalar. As a result, for each i, `matrix_exp_quiz_PM[i, 2:6]` will be right-hand-side only nodes. However, because they only appear on the right-hand side of expressions, there are no calculations associated with it (another way of saying this is that the nodes have no prior).

Could you give more details about the problem you see with the subsequent calculations? You may need to show us your code.

-chris

On Mon, Mar 31, 2025 at 8:08 AM frederic....@gmail.com <frederic....@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> Dear Perry,
>
> I thank you for your answer. The trouble I have is that matrix_exp_quiz_PM is in the constants of the Nimble model (i.e. in the list of constants other than data provided to Nimble). Can it then be considered as a variable? I understood that no. But maybe I did not catch something.
>
> Sincerely,
>
> Frédéric
> Le mercredi 26 mars 2025 à 20:07:04 UTC+1, Perry de Valpine a écrit :
> > Dear Frédéric,
> >
> > A variable in a model does not necessarily have a prior. But I think we should be talking about nodes, because a variable is just a label for an object that may contain one or more nodes. A node that is stochastic and is not data will have a prior.
> >
> > Scalar constants are absorbed completely without creating a variable. Non-scalar constants become variables.
> >

> > > > On Thursday, June 18, 2020 at 2:09:31 PM UTC-6, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > > > Yes.  compileNimble writes C++ code, compiles it, and links it to a  static library that comes with nimble, each result in files.  Also there is a once-per-session compilation step, which is why the first call to compileNimble is always slower than subsequent calls.  The files are normally placed in tempdir(), the temporary directory automatically created by R for each session that is available for use by packages (or the user) and cleaned up upon R exit (usually).  One option would be for you to iterate through your models such that you invoke a new R session for each model.  For example, you could have a primary R session (or other script) that uses system2 to call Rscript to run one case.  That would create separate R process for each case, which should clean up its own tempdir() upon exit.   Another option would be to control where nimble puts its files by using the dirName argument to compileNimble and then adding a step in your code that removes files (curiously named unlink() in R) from wherever you put them.  They shouldn't need to be retained after compileNimble has finished.  If you use that option, you might also want to use nimble:::clearCompiled(obj) after each case, where obj is any object associated with one nimble project, such as the model.  That will attempt to clear memory of the C++ objects from that nimble project.
